topic: D1 Threats / D2 Protecting data — Evaluate (12 mark)
scenario:
Greenfield NHS Trust is a large healthcare organisation serving 500,000 patients. It holds electronic patient records (EPR), appointment data, medical imaging, prescriptions, and staff HR records on its IT systems. Following a government review, the Trust has been told it must achieve Cyber Essentials Plus certification. The IT director must present a full data security improvement plan to the board.

You should consider:
• The external and internal threats to the Trust's data
• The full range of data protection measures available
• The benefits and limitations of each measure
• Which measures should be prioritised and why.
question: Evaluate the data security measures Greenfield NHS Trust should implement to protect patient and staff data, and justify your recommendations.

indicative_content: External threats: ransomware (NHS has been heavily targeted — WannaCry precedent); hackers targeting EPR and medical imaging; phishing targeting clinical and admin staff; DDoS attacks on booking systems; natural disasters

Internal threats: accidental disclosure by staff emailing patient data; use of USB drives by clinical staff; staff accessing inappropriate websites introducing malware; deliberate data theft or leaking of patient records
Measures and evaluation:
Antivirus with real-time scanning and regular updates — essential first line of defence; signature updates needed continuously; heuristic detection for new ransomware variants
Hardware and software firewalls — control network traffic; can segment network so clinical and admin systems are isolated
MFA for all staff accounts — critical after repeated NHS ransomware incidents; reduces impact of stolen credentials from phishing
File permissions and access levels — clinical staff access EPR only; HR staff access HR records; imaging staff access DICOM systems; limits blast radius of any breach
Encryption of stored patient data and data in transit — HTTPS/TLS for all external communications; full disk encryption on mobile devices used by district nurses
Regular offsite/cloud backups with tested restore procedures — enables rapid recovery from ransomware without paying ransom
Physical access control — server rooms secured with biometric or keycard access; CCTV
Staff training and awareness — large organisation with many entry points; training on phishing, password hygiene, and data handling reduces human risk
Digital certificates for all patient-facing portals
Patch management — known vulnerabilities are exploited; WannaCry exploited unpatched Windows systems
Portable device policy — restrict or encrypt USB drives; ban of unapproved devices
Penetration testing — identifies vulnerabilities before attackers

Prioritisation: patch management and antivirus updates most urgent given ransomware history; MFA should be rolled out across all systems; regular tested backups essential for recovery capability; staff training high-value and relatively low-cost

Limitations: cost — NHS budget constraints mean not all measures can be implemented simultaneously; patient care cannot be disrupted during rollout; legacy medical equipment may not support modern encryption or patching; staff resistance to change

Benefits: Cyber Essentials Plus certification required; legal obligations under GDPR and common law duty of confidentiality; patient safety and trust; avoidance of financial and operational disruption caused by ransomware

Conclusion: layered defence-in-depth approach combining technical, procedural, and physical measures is the only effective strategy for an organisation of this scale; immediate priorities are patching, antivirus, MFA, and tested backups; longer-term priorities include full encryption, staff training programme, and physical access controls
